papers.title_in_file: Advantage of Quantum Neural Networks as Quantum Information Decoders
papers.version_note: arXiv:2401.06300v1 [quant-ph] 11 Jan 2024; main text pp.1-6 with the Supplementary Information (pp.S1-S19) in the same text.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper with small simulations that proves scaling bounds on the decoding error of standard QEC and of an unrestricted QNN decoder for stabilizer codes perturbed by local disorder.

existing.note: The improvement is narrower than the stored value says. It is for noisy inputs only; it is the existence of a QNN unitary with no restriction on its architecture (Theorem 3, proved in SI Section IV); and the paper's own 5-qubit noisy simulation (distance d = 3, p = 1) has the same lambda^4 scaling for the QNN as for standard QEC, so no exponent gain appears there.
existing.value: The authors state that they prove, for noisy inputs, that one can always find a QNN whose generalization error is of order lambda raised to four times the ceiling of (d - 2p) over k, as lambda goes to zero, which they call an almost quadratic error improvement over the standard QEC result in Theorem 2; the result is proved without any restriction on the unitary, and for the 5-qubit code with d = 3, p = 1 the lower bound predicts the same scaling as Theorem 2.
existing.anchor: Abstract, p.1; main text p.4; Theorem 3, SI Section IV, p.S11; discussion of Fig. 3(d), p.5
quotes: We then prove that Quantum Neural Network (QNN) decoders provide an almost quadratic improvement on the readout error.
In the presence of noise, QNN provides an almost quadratic error improvement over the standard QEC result in Theorem 2, as detailed in the following theorem.
For noisy inputs, one could always find a QNN such that its generalization error for decoding is εQ(QQNN) = O(λ4⌈(d−2p)/k⌉).
This rigorous result, as well as Theorem 3, were proved without any restrictions on the unitary UQ.
for the 5-qubit code (d = 3, p = 1) simulation, the lower bound in Theorem 3 predicts the same λ4 scaling as in Theorem 2, which the present QNN saturates.
existing.certainty_reason: Theorem 3 is stated informally (p.4) and formally (SI Section IV, p.S11) with its proof; its conditions are quoted. The comparison to Theorem 2 is the authors' own.
existing.reader_inference: The exponent for the QNN, four times ceil((d-2p)/k), against the exponent for QEC, twice ceil((d+1-2p)/k) (Theorem 2, tight for noisy input and generic V), approaches a ratio of two only for large d. For d = 3, p = 1, k = 1 both are four (the paper says so). For d = 5, p = 1, k = 1 they are twelve and eight. The paper's text calls the Proposition 1 lower bound 'the lower bound in Theorem 3'. The proof assumes e_alpha > 0 'for small enough lambda' (SI p.S11), which is not a condition of the theorem as stated. The optimal unitary is built from the exact perturbed codewords, the error-state overlaps and the matrices epsilon and h, and may need many gates (main text p.4).

existing.value: The authors state that their numerical simulations cover codes with 'various distances ranging from 5 to 11 qubits'; the supplement lists four codes, [[5,1,3]], [[7,1,3]], [[9,1,3]] and [[11,1,5]], so the range of 5 to 11 counts physical qubits and the code distances are 3 and 5; the QNN simulations use the 5-qubit code only; the authors focus on imperfect stabilizer codes and leave open whether their formalism extends beyond near-stabilizer codes.

existing.note: The paper's theorem is about the exponent of lambda, as lambda goes to zero, not a stated exponential decay in d. Noiseless input: an upper bound of order lambda^(2 ceil(d/k)). Noisy input with p-local Pauli errors and generic V: a tight (Theta) scaling lambda^(2 ceil((d+1-2p)/k)). The word 'exponentially' is the abstract's reading of that exponent growing with d. The Theta scaling holds under the condition that <W>_mu > 0 (SI Eq. S.64).
existing.value: The authors state in the abstract that they show the decoding error of standard stabilizer-based decoding diminishes exponentially in the distance of the underlying unperturbed code; Theorem 2 gives, as lambda goes to zero, an upper bound of order lambda raised to twice the ceiling of d over k for noiseless input, and a tight scaling of lambda raised to twice the ceiling of (d + 1 - 2p) over k for noisy input and generic V.

existing.reader_inference: The informal statement says 'noisy input (p > 1)', the formal statement says p >= 1 or p > 0 and the 5-qubit simulation uses p = 1, so 'p > 1' reads as a slip. The formal proof ends with a power lambda^(ceil(2(d-2p+1)/k)) in Eq. S.86, the informal statement has 2 ceil((d+1-2p)/k); these differ when (d+1-2p)/k is not an integer (they agree for k = 1). The statement in terms of lambda as lambda goes to zero leaves the constants hidden in the O and Theta, which may depend on d and n (the paper says Theta holds 'while holding everything else fixed (number'), so exponential decay in d at a fixed lambda is not shown by the theorem as stated. For noisy input the exponent shrinks by 4p, so p near d/2 removes the suppression.

assertions.value: The authors set up a general stabilizer quantum code of distance d that encodes a single logical qubit using n physical qubits, with the Hamiltonian H = H0 + lambda V, where H0 is the unperturbed stabilizer Hamiltonian, V is a generic perturbation that is a sum of spatially local terms acting on at most k qubits with k smaller than d, and lambda is a small real parameter that sets the perturbation strength.

This means we can encode information using the two lowest eigenstates |ψ0⟩ and |ψ1⟩ of the perturbed Hamiltonian, H|ψi⟩ = Ei|ψi⟩.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Bravyi, Hastings and Michalakis, that the energy splitting between the two lowest eigenstates of the perturbed Hamiltonian is exponentially small in the stabilizer code's distance d.

assertions.value: The authors use the Brillouin-Wigner perturbative expansion, which needs no separate formula for a degenerate unperturbed spectrum, and state that with an arbitrary choice of degenerate eigenstates the series cannot be treated as a Taylor series because the propagator denominator can be polynomially small in lambda.

This is because the denominator of the propagator Gk can be polynomially small in λ, thus potentially reducing the power of or even cancelling the λ-prefactor.

assertions.value: The paper states Lemma 3: under the uncorrectable-error condition there exist a k-local V and p-local Pauli operators for which a traceless-part norm of the order-(d - 2p) matrix T is greater than zero; the authors read it as showing that, for p = 0, the two lowest eigenstates become non-orthogonal at the d-th order of perturbation theory, and for p > 0 at order d - 2p.

assertions.value: The authors define the QNN decoder as a unitary circuit that takes the encoded state as input and returns the result by measuring the output qubit, equivalent to measuring the operator U† Z0 U for a unitary U and the Pauli-Z operator on the output qubit.
assertions.anchor: Decoding using QNN, main text p.3, Eq. (5)
quotes: Essentially, QNN is a unitary circuit that takes the encoded state as input and returns the result by measuring the output qubit.
QQNN := UQ† Z0UQ.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the QNN decoder.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QNN decoder is used where standard decoding cannot be applied because there is no knowledge of the unperturbed code, and that they assume no knowledge of the perturbed Hamiltonian beyond access to the two spanning codewords of its ground space.
quotes: The standard decoding approaches considered in Theorem 1-2 cannot be applied if one has no knowledge about the unperturbed code.
In the following, we do not assume any knowledge of the perturbed Hamiltonian H beyond the access to the two spanning codewords of its ground space.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of their assumption.
assertions.reader_inference: The numerical QNN is trained on labeled states (next assertion); the optimal unitary of Theorem 3 uses exact codewords and the overlap matrices.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the absence of noise a QNN decoder, unlike standard QEC, can achieve arbitrary precision at sufficiently large depths, because for any pair of codewords there is a unitary mapping them to a product state with different states of the target qubit; Remark 6 states the same for the Theorem 3 QNN with no constraint on the architecture.
assertions.anchor: Main text p.4; Remark 6, SI Section V, p.S16
quotes: In the absence of noise in the input, QNN decoding, unlike standard QEC, can achieve arbitrary precision at sufficiently large depths.
This is because, for arbitrary pair of codewords, there exists a unitary UQ that transforms them into a product state with different states of the target qubit.
Remark 6 For noiseless input (p = 0), the QNN considered in Theorem 3 can decode input states with arbitrary accuracy, provided that there is no constraint on its architecture.
assertions.certainty_reason: A one-sentence existence argument and a remark; no formal theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: Theorem 3 at p = 0 gives only the order lambda to four times ceil(d/k), so 'arbitrary accuracy' is a different statement, resting on the unitary being built from the exact codewords.

assertions.value: The paper states Theorem 3 (formal): for every Pauli observable among X, Y and Z there is a unitary U such that the generalization error of the QNN observable U† Z0 U is of order lambda raised to four times the ceiling of (d - 2p) over k.
assertions.anchor: Theorem 3 (informal), main text p.4; Theorem 3 (Formal), SI Section IV, p.S11
quotes: For noisy inputs, one could always find a QNN such that its generalization error for decoding is εQ(QQNN) = O(λ4⌈(d−2p)/k⌉).
Theorem 3 (Formal) Define the quantum neural network observable QQNN = UQ† Z0UQ, where UQ is a unitary transformation and Z0 is the Pauli Z operator on the target qubit.
Then for every Pauli observable Q ∈ {X, Y, Z} there exists a corresponding unitary UQ such that the error εQ(QQNN)) = O(λ4⌈(d−2p)/k⌉).
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement and conditions quoted from the informal and formal versions; proof in SI Section IV.
assertions.reader_inference: It is an existence result for an upper bound, with no bound on the number of gates and no training procedure.

assertions.value: The paper's proof of the QNN decoding theorem builds nearly orthonormal states from the error-corrupted codewords with a correction of order lambda to the q, with q the ceiling of (d - 2p) over k, and assumes that the eigenvalues of the matrix of overlaps are positive for small enough lambda; the optimal unitary follows by orthonormalizing these states.

where the last O(λ2q) term can be decided by the Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization procedure applied to the set of vectors {|vαk⟩}.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of the proof's construction and one assumption it adds; not a result of its own.
assertions.reader_inference: The positivity of e_alpha is not a condition of the theorem as stated.

assertions.value: The authors state that achieving the optimal QNN may involve numerous gates and a complex optimization process, and that it is an interesting future direction to find whether logarithmic-depth QNNs such as convolutional networks can saturate the bound in Theorem 3.
assertions.anchor: Main text p.4 and Discussion p.6
quotes: In practice, achieving this optimal QNN may involve numerous gates and a complex optimization process.
An interesting future direction is to find whether it is possible to construct logarithmic-depth QNNs such as convolutional NNs that saturate the bound in Theorem 3.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of a limit and an open problem.

assertions.value: The paper states Proposition 1 (informal): for noisy inputs with a distribution that is symmetric under a shift of the phase by π and label values of plus or minus one, for generic V, every QNN unitary must have generalization error bounded below by order lambda raised to four times the ceiling of (d - 2p) over k.
quotes: Proposition 1 (informal) Consider noisy inputs with distribution µ(θ, ϕ) = µ(θ, ϕ + π) and label values fQ(θ, ϕ) = ±1.
Then for generic V , all QNN unitaries UQ must satisfy εQ(QQNN) = Ω(λ4⌈(d−2p)/k⌉).
Here we use Ω notation to indicate asymptotic lower bound as λ → 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement and conditions quoted from the informal and formal versions.
assertions.reader_inference: Together with Theorem 3 it makes the exponent of the best QNN exactly four times ceil((d-2p)/k). The label values of plus or minus one hold for the logical basis states of the Bloch sphere (poles and axes), not for a general input.

assertions.value: The paper states Proposition 1 (formal): under the conditions of Theorem 3, for any input distribution with label values of plus or minus one, symmetric under a π shift of the phase, and such that a weighted fourth-power expectation of the matrix T between a state and its phase-shifted partner is positive for all shifts, every QNN unitary has generalization error bounded below by order lambda raised to four times the ceiling of (d - 2p) over k.

assertions.value: The authors state in Remark 5 that the assumption of the positive weighted fourth-power expectation is a generality condition, that the earlier technical lemma shows the matrix T is not trivial for some perturbations and noise, and that the condition fails only for a fine-tuned choice of input states.

More generally, there is no particular reason to believe that this expression vanishes for generic parameters of the problem.

assertions.value: The authors describe their QNN as two blocks: a correction circuit of local two-qubit gates in a brickwork pattern of depth dC, and a decoding circuit that is a convolutional network of O(log n) layers of two-qubit unitaries, discarding half the qubits after each layer; each two-qubit unitary is the exponential of a sum over Pauli products with trainable angles.
quotes: Our network, trainable to sample in logical Q-basis, consists of two blocks shown in Fig. 3(a): correction circuit CQ (blue) and decoding circuit DQ (green).
The correction circuit is composed of local two-qubit gates forming the brickwork pattern of depth dC.
In turn, the decoding circuit is a convolutional network consisting of O(log n) layers of two-qubit unitaries, discarding half the qubits after each layer, similar to previous proposals [30, 39].
where φαkβ ∈ [0, 2π] are trainable angles and σα are single-qubit Pauli matrices.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' description of their architecture.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QNN is trained on a limited set of training and validation states in the code space with the corresponding labels (θ, ϕ), that one can assume such access because the ground space can be prepared adiabatically in experimental settings, and that the QNN is optimized on the training data with the generalization error as the objective.

in experimental settings. We optimize the QNN with objective function εQ(QQNN) (Eq. (3)) on the training data.

assertions.reader_inference: Training needs states with known logical labels; the QNN is Hamiltonian-agnostic but not label-agnostic.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QNN was trained on 1600 training examples and validated on ten times as many independently drawn samples; dC = 4 gave 255 parameters, each two-qubit unitary having 15 free angles; optimization used BFGS with a maximum of 105 iterations and tolerance 10−15 (exponents printed flat, read as ten to the fifth and ten to the minus fifteenth); for the noisy case one of 16 single-qubit Pauli errors including the identity was applied at random.

quotes: After training, we test our QNN on NV = 10 × NT samples withheld from the training but independently drawn from the same distribution.
In Fig.3(b)-(d), we have NT = 1600 training examples.
Each two-qubit unitary Uk (Eq. (6)) contains 42−1 = 15 independent parameters.

we chose dC = 4, which corresponds to 255 parameters. We optimize these parameters with BFGS method using the SciPy optimize library (maximum number of iterations is 105, tolerance for termination is 10−15).
we randomly apply one of the M = 16 possible single-qubit Pauli errors (including the identity) to each of the sample states in both training and validation set.

assertions.value: The authors report that optimizing with stochastic gradient descent tends to yield larger decoding error, incompatible with the accuracy required by the comparison with perturbation theory, and so use BFGS.

assertions.certainty_reason: An unquantified observation.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the QNN simulations of Fig. 3 they use a uniform 1-local perturbation equal to the sum over qubits of X plus Z, in contrast to the random Gaussian-unitary-ensemble perturbations used for the standard-decoding simulations.
quotes: We provide numerical simulation results in Fig. 3, where we study a uniform 1-local perturbation Vi =
in=1(Xi + Zi).
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of the Fig. 3 setup.
assertions.reader_inference: One fixed structured perturbation; the theorems are for generic V.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QNN architecture with dC = 4 can decode noiseless inputs of the five-qubit code and achieves superior performance compared to the standard decoding schemes of Theorems 1-2 regardless of the perturbation strength, outperforming them across nearly two orders of magnitude in lambda, and that deeper architectures reduce the error further at the cost of longer training.
assertions.anchor: Main text p.5; Fig. 3(b)-(c) caption, p.4
quotes: Fig. 3(b)-(c) suggest that our QNN architecture (C = 4) can decode noiseless inputs and achieves superior performance compared to standard decoding schemes discussed in Theorems 1-2, regardless of the perturbation strength.
Panels (b)-(c) demonstrate that QNN significantly outperforms the standard approaches across nearly two orders of magnitude in λ.
The QNN error can be further reduced by considering deeper architectures at the cost of longer training times.
assertions.certainty_reason: A numerical result for one code, one perturbation, one architecture; data points in a figure.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Regardless of the perturbation strength' is stated for the range simulated.

assertions.value: The authors report for the noisy 5-qubit-code simulation (d = 3, p = 1) that the lower bound predicts the same lambda to the fourth scaling for QNN and standard QEC and the present QNN saturates it, that QNN performance is comparable to standard QEC for small lambda and becomes superior for large lambda, and that Fig. 3(d) confirms that the scalings agree with the analytical predictions of Theorems 2-3.
assertions.anchor: Main text p.5; Fig. 3(d) caption, p.4
quotes: Incidentally, for the 5-qubit code (d = 3, p = 1) simulation, the lower bound in Theorem 3 predicts the same λ4 scaling as in Theorem 2, which the present QNN saturates.
Intriguingly, while QNN performance is comparable to that of standard QEC for small λ, and becomes superior for large λ.
Panel (d) confirms that the scaling of standard QEC and QNN agree with our analytical predictions in Theorems 2-3.
assertions.certainty_reason: One code, one noise model, one architecture; data in a figure.
assertions.reader_inference: No exponent advantage is observed in this run, by the paper's own account; the advantage is at large lambda, outside the lambda-to-zero regime of the theorems.

assertions.value: The paper reports no QNN simulation for any code other than the 5-qubit code: the QNN figures are titled for the 5-qubit code, and the authors state only that one can potentially achieve better scaling with a larger-distance code such as the [[11,1,5]] code.
assertions.anchor: Fig. 3 caption p.4; main text p.5; SI Section VI.C.1, p.S18
quotes: FIG. 3. QNN performance for 5-qubit code.
However, with QNN one can potentially achieve better scaling by considering larger code distances such as the [[11,1,5]] code.
Specializing the general architecture in Fig.3(a) to 5-qubit code, we use the 5-qubit QNN architecture in Fig. S1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own scope: QNN simulations are for the 5-qubit code (caption and SI).
assertions.reader_inference: The QNN advantage at higher distance is a theoretical existence result; it is not tested by any QNN run in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that their result illustrates that sequential error correction and measurement of the logical operator at the end of the circuit can be implemented by applying a QNN unitary and a single-qubit measurement without any ancilla, and that the approach requires no knowledge of the Hamiltonian, which standard QEC methods need.
quotes: Meanwhile, this approach does not require any knowledge of the Hamiltonian, as needed in standard QEC methods.

Also, this result illustrates that sequential error correction and measurement of the logical operator at the end of the circuit can be implemented by applying a QNN unitary and single-qubit measurement without using any ancilla.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' reading of a simulation result.

assertions.value: The authors report that a shallow network (dC = 1) fails to learn noisy samples even for the ideal stabilizer code, that the generalization error decreases as dC grows with a critical depth at which the scatter plot suddenly falls on the diagonal, that at dC = 4 the QNN expectation matches the target, and that the correction circuit is not equivalent to standard QEC; for dC = 4 the typical optimization time is around one hour on a four-core CPU.
assertions.anchor: SI Section VI.C.2, pp.S18-S19, Fig. S1
quotes: We find that for a shallow network, e.g., dC = 1, even for ideal stabilizer code (λ = 0), the QNN fails to learn noisy samples (Fig. S1(b)).
We observe that at dC = 4 the scatter plot falls on the diagonal (⟨XQNN⟩ ≈ fX ) (Fig. S1(e)).
but we emphasis that CQ is not really performing the error-correction equivalent to the standarad QEC.
For dC = 4, the typical optimization time is around one hour on a intel i7 @ 1.90GHz 4 Cores CPU (without parallelization).

assertions.value: The authors report that for noiseless inputs (the task of Fig. 3(c)) generalization performance improves with depth dC = 2, 3, 4, that a translationally invariant architecture with 75 parameters, sharing parameters within a layer, performs worse than the 255-parameter dC = 4 architecture, and that all depths and architectures have roughly the same constant scaling with lambda, which they say suggests a robust scaling behavior.
assertions.anchor: SI Section VI.C.2, p.S19, Fig. S2
quotes: In Fig. S2, we consider different depths dC = 2, 3, 4, and find the generalization performance improves as depth increases.
e.g., dC = 4 (Trans. Inv. ) has 75 parameters, less than the 255 parameters in dC = 4.
We find that the generalization performance of this architecture is worse than that of the dC = 4 architecture we used in Fig. S1

It is worth noticing that all the different depths and architectures considered in Fig. S1 has roughly the same constant scaling with λ, suggesting a robust scaling behavior regardless of the specific architecture used.
assertions.certainty_reason: Observations from one code and one task.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing McClean et al. and Cerezo et al., that training quantum neural networks is known to suffer from the barren plateau problem, where gradients become exponentially small in the system size, and that it has been recently demonstrated that this can be circumvented with logarithmic-depth convolutional networks with local output observables.
quotes: training quantum neural networks is known to suffer from the barren plateau problem, where gradients become exponentially small in the system size
Nevertheless, it has been recently demonstrated that the barren plateau problem can be circumvented by utilizing logarithmic-depth convolutional networks with local output observables [39].
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to references [38] and [39].
assertions.reader_inference: Reference [39]'s title in this paper's list is 'Cost function dependent barren plateaus in shallow parametrized quantum circuits'.

assertions.value: The authors state that if the combined QNN has an overall logarithmic depth, they expect it does not suffer from the barren plateau problem and can be efficiently optimized.
quotes: If the combined network has an overall logarithmic depth, we expect that it does not suffer from the barren plateau problem [38] and can be efficiently optimized.
assertions.certainty_reason: An expectation stated without argument or measurement.
assertions.reader_inference: The simulated 5-qubit QNN has 255 parameters, was trained with BFGS, and needed about an hour; no scaling in n is measured.

assertions.value: The authors state that they show simple measurements of logical operators are not sufficient to achieve fault tolerance, and that a sequence of stabilizer measurements followed by error corrections are required to decode even noiseless input states.
quotes: In particular, we show that simple measurements of logical operators are not sufficient to achieve fault tolerance, and that a sequence of stabilizer measurements followed by error corrections are required to decode even noiseless input states.
assertions.certainty_reason: A summary sentence; Theorems 1 and 2 support the first half for the specific decoders they treat.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Required' is not proved: Theorem 3 and Remark 6 give a QNN decoder with better error that does not use syndrome measurements.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Cong et al., Locher et al. and Cao et al., that parameterized quantum circuits, also called quantum neural networks, have been demonstrated to recognize quantum states in different phases and perform QEC.
quotes: strated that parameterized quantum circuits [5, 34, 35], also called Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs), can recognize quantum states in different phases and perform QEC [30, 36, 37].
assertions.certainty_reason: Results attributed to references [30], [36], [37].

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they developed a theoretical framework for decoding stabilizer codes perturbed by disorder, proved general performance bounds for standard QEC versus QNN decoding, and that their results reveal universal scaling of the decoding error for arbitrary code distances and suggest a provable advantage of QNNs over standard QEC for decoding realistic codes with large code distances.
quotes: We proved general performance bounds regarding the decoding errors of standard QEC versus QNN decoding techniques for such codes.
Our results reveal universal scaling behaviors of the decoding error for arbitrary code distances, and suggests a provable advantage of using QNNs over standard QEC methods for
decoding realistic codes with large code distances.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion; its support is Theorems 1 to 3 and Proposition 1.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Universal' rests on constants hidden in the O and Theta and on generic V; the advantage is an exponent comparison as lambda goes to zero.

assertions.value: The authors state as open problems whether their formalism can be extended beyond near-stabilizer codes, and how the structure and depth of QNNs affect practical decoding performance.
quotes: While we focus on imperfect stabilizer codes, an immediate question is whether our formalism can be extended beyond near-stabilizer codes.
In addition, how does the structure and depth of QNNs affect practical decoding performance remains an important open problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of open problems.
